challenges.opponent_argument: R.C. 5321.01(A) defines a 'tenant' as a person entitled under a rental agreement to exclusive use and occupancy. Alice Stone had no rental agreement and shared the residence with the owner, so she lacked exclusive possession and was not a tenant. Therefore, R.C. 5321.15 and Chapter 1923 do not apply to her.
challenges.why_it_matters: If Alice was not a tenant, the statutory prohibition on self-help lockouts does not apply, and the appellees could exclude her without eviction process.

While Cazeau could revoke or terminate Alice's at will occupation of his property, he was statutorily prohibited from distraining her property and access to the residence without

legal_sources.title: Ohio Eviction and Landlord-Tenant Law — C. Tenant
legal_sources.citation: Ohio Eviction and Landlord-Tenant Law, 2022-06 (Sixth Edition), VI. Ohio Landlord-Tenant Act, > C. Tenant (PDF pp. 332–335)
queries: Ohio cohabitant guest licensee not tenant eviction statutes Chapter 1923 R.C. 5321.15 no exclusive possession self-help lockout owner may exclude occupant at will

challenges.judge_assessment: This identifies the brief's central statutory vulnerability. The cited source supports the narrower proposition that R.C. Chapter 5321 defines a tenant by entitlement under a rental agreement to use and occupy residential premises to the exclusion of others. The record summarized in the brief identifies cohabitation at the owner's request, but no rent, lease, other rental agreement, or exclusive right against the owner. Thus R.C. 5321.15 may not apply. But the attack overreaches in treating that conclusion as automatically eliminating Chapter 1923: R.C. 1923.02 is not facially confined to statutory tenants and includes certain occupiers. The advocate risks losing the R.C. 5321.15 claim and statutory damages/fees, while a separate Chapter 1923 or common-law theory may remain depending on Alice's precise possessory status.
challenges.suggested_response: Even if Alice Stone did not hold a written lease, the appellees were not free to oust her by self-help. R.C. 1923.02 reaches an occupier of lands or tenements without color of title and unlawful, forcible detention of real property; it is not limited on its face to parties who can prove a formal lease. On this record, at minimum, Alice was an occupant in possession, and appellees’ remedy was to proceed by lawful process rather than changing the locks and excluding her from the premises. To the extent the Court concludes Alice’s occupancy also brought her within Chapter 5321, R.C. 5321.15 independently barred the lockout and the recovery of possession by self-help.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Revise the argument to stop treating Alice as a statutory tenant unless the record supports a rental agreement or another source of exclusive possessory rights. Frame the claim primarily as a wrongful dispossession of an occupier under R.C. 1923.02, and present R.C. 5321.15 only in the alternative if the Court accepts tenant status.

challenges.opponent_argument: The brief's reliance on Sutherland v. Moore is misplaced because an occupant at will who pays no rent and has no lease is not a tenant at sufferance entitled to Chapter 1923 process. A tenant at sufferance arises when a tenant holds over after a lease expires. Alice never had a lease. She was a mere licensee whose permission could be revoked at any time.
challenges.why_it_matters: Without a tenancy, the eviction statutes do not apply, and the lockout was lawful.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a substantial attack on the brief's unsupported classification of Alice as a tenant at sufferance. The cited source supports the statutory definition of tenant and highlights the absence of a rental agreement and exclusive occupancy. The record as presented contains no prior leasehold from which a conventional holdover tenancy plainly arose. The brief asserts rather than demonstrates that an occupant at will automatically becomes a tenant at sufferance upon revocation. Still, the source does not establish the attack's categorical claim that every rent-free cohabitant is a mere licensee or that Chapter 1923 is unavailable, because Chapter 1923 reaches some occupiers beyond statutory tenants. The advocate stands to lose the legal bridge from cohabitation to protected tenancy; that could defeat R.C. 5321.15 and materially weaken the wrongful-ouster theory.
challenges.suggested_response: The point is not that Alice Stone held over under a lease. The point is that she was in possession of the residence, the appellees disputed that possession, and they could not end the dispute by changing the locks and posting notices declaring her a trespasser. Chapter 1923 provides the statutory process for recovering possession from an occupier and for unlawful, forcible detention of property. Whatever label is attached to Alice’s occupancy, appellees were required to use that process rather than resorting to self-help.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Delete the unsupported statement that Alice became a tenant at sufferance by operation of law. Use the record-supported point that she was occupying the residence, appellees revoked her access, and Chapter 1923 required lawful process before dispossession.

challenges.opponent_argument: Alice failed to present evidence that appellees exercised dominion over her property; her affidavit only states she was locked out. Under the summary judgment standard, she needed to set forth specific facts showing conversion, which she did not. The mere inability to access the residence does not constitute wrongful control or dominion.
challenges.why_it_matters: The conversion claim fails for lack of evidence, so summary judgment was proper.

legal_sources.citation: 2014 CVG 001938 (Cleveland Mun. Ct., Housing Div. Nov. 24-25, 2014)
queries: Ohio summary judgment self-serving affidavit conclusory allegations no specific facts essential element Dresher Burt Anderson Liberty nonmovant burden

challenges.judge_assessment: The legal point that conversion requires evidence of dominion is sound, but the attack misstates the record by saying Alice showed only a lockout. Her affidavit, as described in the brief, identifies specific belongings, repeated attempts to retrieve them, repeated re-locking, and that appellees kept and never returned the items. Together with Nixon's control of access, those facts permit an inference of control inconsistent with Alice's ownership. The brief's phrase that the items were 'kept' is somewhat conclusory, and it does not identify an express demand and refusal or disposition of the goods; but an express demand is not necessarily indispensable where the alleged possession was wrongful from the outset. On summary judgment, the inference is sufficient unless appellees produced unrebutted evidence showing lack of possession, access, or refusal. The advocate risks little by raising the narrower evidentiary gap, but overstatement undermines credibility.
challenges.suggested_response: The summary-judgment record, viewed in Alice Stone’s favor, did more than show a lockout. Alice testified that suits, dresses, craft materials, and personal papers remained in the residence; that she attempted to recover them; that the locks were changed again while her belongings were still inside; and that appellees never returned the remaining property. Those facts permit a reasonable inference that appellees exercised control over Alice’s property inconsistent with her ownership rights. At the very least, they created a genuine issue of fact on conversion that could not be resolved on summary judgment.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not say the record conclusively proves conversion. Tighten the point to what the summary-judgment record permits: repeated lockouts, identified personal property left in the residence, and appellees’ failure to return it create a genuine issue of dominion inconsistent with Alice’s rights.

challenges.opponent_argument: The appellees changed the locks to secure the residence of the ailing owner, not for the purpose of recovering possession. R.C. 5321.15 requires an act 'for the purpose of recovering possession.' The brief's facts show Edwin's hospitalization, supporting a security purpose. Without intent to force a move, there is no violation, as recognized in Brown v. Williams.
challenges.why_it_matters: Even if R.C. 5321.15 applied, the appellees' intent was protective, so no statutory violation occurred.

challenges.judge_assessment: R.C. 5321.15's purpose element is real, and Brown v. Williams supports the proposition that an interference not intended to force a tenant out may fall outside that provision. But the proposed factual inference is not supported on this record. Hospitalization alone does not show a security motive, while the contemporaneous notices said Alice was trespassing, ordered her not to enter, and announced that all locks had been changed; the locks were changed repeatedly as she tried to retrieve belongings; and appellees later served a notice to quit. Those facts strongly support a possession-recovery purpose. At most, competing motives would create a fact issue, not justify summary judgment for appellees. Pressing the attack as an established fact risks appearing to ask the appellate court to draw inferences against the nonmovant.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellees cannot obtain summary judgment by recasting the repeated lock changes as a mere security measure. The contemporaneous notices told Alice Stone that she was trespassing, ordered her not to enter the house, and stated that all locks had been changed; when Alice returned to retrieve her belongings, the locks were changed again; and a notice to quit followed only after her exclusion. From those facts, a factfinder could infer that the lock changes were undertaken for the purpose of recovering possession, not simply to secure the property while Edwin Cazeau was hospitalized. At minimum, the record presents a factual dispute on appellees’ purpose that precluded summary judgment.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not argue that appellees’ motive was security as an established fact. Instead, acknowledge any claimed security purpose as a disputed inference and emphasize the contrary evidence showing a possession-recovery purpose.

judge_assessments.assessment: The legal point that conversion requires evidence of dominion is sound, but the attack misstates the record by saying Alice showed only a lockout. Her affidavit, as described in the brief, identifies specific belongings, repeated attempts to retrieve them, repeated re-locking, and that appellees kept and never returned the items. Together with Nixon's control of access, those facts permit an inference of control inconsistent with Alice's ownership. The brief's phrase that the items were 'kept' is somewhat conclusory, and it does not identify an express demand and refusal or disposition of the goods; but an express demand is not necessarily indispensable where the alleged possession was wrongful from the outset. On summary judgment, the inference is sufficient unless appellees produced unrebutted evidence showing lack of possession, access, or refusal. The advocate risks little by raising the narrower evidentiary gap, but overstatement undermines credibility.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief defines conversion, identifies the property left inside, says appellees kept and never returned it, and argues that Nixon repeatedly changed the locks while Alice was trying to reclaim it, thereby exercising wrongful dominion.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The actual affidavit and appellees' Civ.R. 56 materials, plus Ohio cases on conversion by denial of access to goods and when demand and refusal are required, would determine whether the inference is sufficient.

judge_assessments.assessment: R.C. 5321.15's purpose element is real, and Brown v. Williams supports the proposition that an interference not intended to force a tenant out may fall outside that provision. But the proposed factual inference is not supported on this record. Hospitalization alone does not show a security motive, while the contemporaneous notices said Alice was trespassing, ordered her not to enter, and announced that all locks had been changed; the locks were changed repeatedly as she tried to retrieve belongings; and appellees later served a notice to quit. Those facts strongly support a possession-recovery purpose. At most, competing motives would create a fact issue, not justify summary judgment for appellees. Pressing the attack as an established fact risks appearing to ask the appellate court to draw inferences against the nonmovant.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief expressly says the notices forbade entry and labeled Alice a trespasser, the locks were repeatedly changed to oust her, and the notice to quit came only after exclusion.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The appellees' affidavits and any evidence stating why the locks were changed would determine whether a genuine purpose dispute exists.

judge_assessments.assessment: The cited source supports the reciprocal Civ.R. 56 burden, but not disregarding an affidavit merely because it is self-serving. The attack also misreads the response: the affidavit reportedly supplied specific dates, notices, lock changes, retrieval efforts, item descriptions, and nonreturn. Whether Alice had a rental agreement or exclusive possession is principally a legal-status problem, not proof that every factual assertion was conclusory. A court would address the particular missing element rather than reject the affidavit wholesale. The attack would cost credibility without materially improving appellees' position.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief details specific affidavit facts and exhibits and correctly invokes Dresher's initial burden, although it incompletely discusses the nonmovant's reciprocal burden.

judge_assessments.assessment: The first sentence duplicates the serious tenant-status objection in a1. The additional assertion that an owner may use self-help against a licensee is not supported by either cited source. Source 2 concerns lockouts of tenants, and source 6 defines tenant; neither establishes affirmative self-help rights against licensees or negates the broader categories in R.C. Chapter 1923. Because the attack combines a supported point already captured elsewhere with an unsupported dispositive leap, it should not be advanced in this form.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief argues that Alice was at least an occupant at will or tenant at sufferance and that R.C. 1923.02 independently required forcible-entry-and-detainer process.

judge_assessments.assessment: The cited source says changing locks for the purpose of recovering possession is prohibited as to a tenant; it does not support treating a pre-process lockout as lawful because a notice was later served. The record, viewed favorably to Alice, shows the opposite sequence: repeated exclusion occurred before the notice to quit, and the police allegedly instructed appellees to file for eviction because they could not bar access. A notice to quit is preliminary notice, not completed judicial process, and does not retroactively cure a prior lockout. Calling the locks a temporary security measure lacks record support.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief squarely answers this by emphasizing that locks were changed before the notice to quit and that later notice did not constitute completed Chapter 1923 process.

judge_assessments.assessment: It is fair that a police officer's statement is not a legal adjudication of tenancy or an admission by appellees. But the brief does not treat it as dispositive; it uses the statement as corroboration that access remained disputed and no lawful eviction had occurred. The cited source does not address the evidentiary meaning of police reluctance or notices to quit. The attack therefore narrows one supporting fact but does not answer the lock changes, written no-entry notices, or timing of process.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief presents the police statement as part of the chronology and separately relies on Alice's occupancy facts, statutory provisions, admissions, and written notices.

judge_assessments.assessment: The abstract proposition is correct: nominal damages preserve a conversion claim only after liability is established. But the brief itself says exactly that by quoting, 'Once conversion has been established,' and separately argues dominion and wrongfulness in u72. This attack merely assumes the disputed premise that no liability evidence exists and adds nothing to the genuine conversion issue. A court would reach damages only after resolving liability.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief conditions nominal damages on established conversion and separately offers facts and authority on conversion liability.

judge_assessments.assessment: The summary-judgment rule is supported, but the factual premise is not verifiable from the supplied record because the motion itself is not provided and the attack cites no record material showing what appellees specifically pointed to. It also conflates distinct claims: rental agreement and exclusive possession concern the statutory lockout theory, while wrongful control concerns conversion. Alice did produce evidence of lockouts, belongings, retrieval efforts, and nonreturn. The court cannot affirm based on an asserted Dresher showing that is absent from the record presented here.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says appellees merely claimed Alice could prove no facts, while Alice responded with an affidavit and exhibits; it argues appellees failed to affirmatively negate ouster without process.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is the strongest attack, but only in part. Sources 22 and 24 support that R.C. 5321.15 regulates conduct by a landlord against a tenant and gives the tenant the remedy. The brief does not identify a lease, rent, or other evidence establishing that Alice was a statutory tenant; indeed, it concedes she was at least a social guest and labels her an occupant at will or sufferance without analyzing the statutory definitions. That is a substantial gap in the R.C. 5321.15 theory. The cited sources do not, however, establish the attack's further assertion that the absence of a written rental agreement or rent necessarily defeats tenant status, nor do they dispose of the separate Chapter 1923 theory concerning an occupier or tenant at sufferance. If appellees establish under the governing 2005 definitions that Alice was not a tenant, appellant likely loses the R.C. 5321.15 claim and its statutory damages and fees, but not automatically the conversion claim or every possible unlawful-exclusion theory.

attacks_proposed.argument: R.C. 5321.15 prohibits only a 'landlord' from excluding a 'tenant' by self-help. Alice was not a tenant under Ohio's Landlord-Tenant Act because there was no rental agreement; she was at most a licensee or social guest. The protections of R.C. 5321.15 do not extend to her, and the trial court correctly found no genuine issue on this essential element.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If R.C. 5321.15 does not apply, the lockout was not statutorily unlawful, and the wrongful eviction claim fails as a matter of law, supporting summary judgment.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief's characterization of the lockout as 'wrongful' assumes that Alice had a legal right to occupy the premises. Because she was not a tenant, Edwin Cazeau, as the owner, could revoke her license to be on the property at any time without resort to judicial process. The self-help lockout was therefore not 'wrongful' under R.C. 5321.15 or any other statute.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Without a wrongful act, the exclusion claim collapses, and summary judgment was proper.

attacks_proposed.argument: Conversion requires an exercise of dominion or control over property inconsistent with the owner's rights. The brief does not allege that the appellees used, sold, or destroyed Alice's belongings; they merely changed the locks to secure the premises. Mere denial of access to the premises, without more, does not constitute conversion of personal property left inside, especially when the owner's right to be on the premises has been lawfully terminated.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the conversion claim is legally insufficient, the trial court's summary judgment on that claim must be affirmed.

attacks_proposed.argument: The availability of nominal damages presupposes that conversion has been established. Because Alice failed to present evidence of a wrongful exercise of dominion over her property, no conversion occurred, and the dispute over damages is irrelevant. Summary judgment was appropriate because the record lacks proof of an essential element of the conversion claim.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Even if damages were disputed, the absence of liability means the claim cannot survive, and the trial court's decision should be upheld.

attacks_proposed.argument: Although review is de novo, the appellate court is limited to the Civ.R. 56 materials. Those materials show no rental agreement, no payment of rent, and no other indicia of a landlord-tenant relationship. The trial court correctly determined that Alice failed to raise a genuine issue on the essential element of her status as a tenant, and the de novo standard does not alter that conclusion.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The standard of review does not rescue the brief if the record lacks evidence on a dispositive element; the summary judgment should be affirmed.

attacks_proposed.argument: Describing Alice and Edwin as 'consorts' or 'house companions' does not establish a legal tenancy. Ohio law requires a rental agreement or at least the payment of rent to create a landlord-tenant relationship. The brief's factual assertions about cohabitation are legally insufficient to trigger the protections of R.C. 5321.15 or Chapter 1923.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The relationship description is irrelevant to the legal claim; without a tenancy, the entire statutory framework the brief relies on is inapplicable.

attacks_proposed.argument: Even if Cathryn Nixon acted as Edwin's attorney in fact, her authority did not extend to violating R.C. 5321.15 if that statute applied. However, because Alice was not a tenant, the lockout was not unlawful, and the scope of Cathryn's agency is immaterial. The trial court could properly disregard this argument as irrelevant to the essential elements of Alice's claims.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The agency argument does not create a genuine issue if the underlying conduct was not wrongful; summary judgment remains proper.

attacks_proposed.argument: The trial court did not err because Alice failed to present evidence that she was a 'tenant' entitled to the protections of R.C. 5321.15. The appellees met their initial burden under Dresher by pointing to the absence of a rental agreement, and Alice's affidavit did not create a genuine issue on that essential element. Summary judgment was therefore required.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the record lacks evidence on an essential element, the grant of summary judgment must be affirmed, and the case should not be remanded.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief's reliance on Coward v. Fleming is misplaced. That case involved a tenant at sufferance in a landlord-tenant relationship, not a cohabitant or social guest. Moreover, Coward predates the enactment of R.C. 5321.15 and does not address the statutory definition of 'tenant.' The trial court was not bound by Coward in this context.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If Coward is distinguishable, the brief loses its primary authority for the proposition that self-help is unlawful against an occupant at will, weakening the wrongful eviction claim.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief's assertion that the lockout was 'wrongful' is a legal conclusion, not a fact. The record shows that Edwin Cazeau, as the owner, had the right to exclude Alice, a mere licensee, without process. The trial court was entitled to view the evidence in the light most favorable to Alice but still conclude that no genuine issue existed on the wrongfulness of the exclusion.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the exclusion was not wrongful as a matter of law, the entire case fails, and summary judgment was correctly entered.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is the strongest attack, but only in part. Sources 22 and 24 support that R.C. 5321.15 regulates conduct by a landlord against a tenant and gives the tenant the remedy. The brief does not identify a lease, rent, or other evidence establishing that Alice was a statutory tenant; indeed, it concedes she was at least a social guest and labels her an occupant at will or sufferance without analyzing the statutory definitions. That is a substantial gap in the R.C. 5321.15 theory. The cited sources do not, however, establish the attack's further assertion that the absence of a written rental agreement or rent necessarily defeats tenant status, nor do they dispose of the separate Chapter 1923 theory concerning an occupier or tenant at sufferance. If appellees establish under the governing 2005 definitions that Alice was not a tenant, appellant likely loses the R.C. 5321.15 claim and its statutory damages and fees, but not automatically the conversion claim or every possible unlawful-exclusion theory.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says Alice lived at the residence at Edwin's request for a substantial period, characterizes her as an occupant at will or sufferance and a tenant at sufferance, and invokes R.C. 1923.02(A)(5)-(6), Coward, and R.C. 5321.15. It does not explain why those facts make her a 'tenant' under Chapter 5321.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The decisive research is the 2005 version of R.C. 5321.01's definitions of landlord, tenant, and rental agreement; Ohio authority addressing rent-free cohabitants or licensees; and the full text and later treatment of Coward v. Fleming.

judge_assessments.assessment: Source 22 establishes that R.C. 5321.15 protects tenants from landlord self-help; it does not establish that an owner may use self-help against every licensee or social guest, or that no other statute or common-law rule requires process. The attack also bypasses the brief's separate reliance on the broad 'occupier' language in R.C. 1923.02(A)(5)-(6) and Coward's tenant-at-sufferance proposition. The court could examine Alice's legal status, but it could not accept the asserted right of self-help from this authority alone. As framed, the attack overclaims and would not dispose of conversion in any event.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief argues that Alice was an occupant at will or sufferance protected by Chapter 1923 and that even a tenant at sufferance may be removed only through forcible-entry-and-detainer process.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Research Ohio authority specifically addressing revocation of a residential license or cohabitant's permission to occupy and whether self-help exclusion is permitted outside Chapter 5321.

judge_assessments.assessment: The attack misreads both the conversion definition and the record described in the brief. Conversion does not invariably require use, sale, or destruction; wrongful control inconsistent with the owner's rights is the stated test. Alice's affidavit allegedly says appellees repeatedly blocked her attempts to retrieve identified belongings, kept those items, and never returned them. That evidence, if competent and unrebutted for summary-judgment purposes, is more than a bare allegation that the premises were secured. Source 51 does not support the proposed limitation and instead describes liability where a landlord unlawfully seized occupants' possessions. Appellees can contest wrongfulness, possession, demand, or attribution, but this categorical attack would land poorly.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief identifies suits, dresses, craft materials, and personal papers; says Alice attempted to reclaim them; and says appellees kept and never returned them after repeatedly changing the locks.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The complete summary-judgment affidavits and Ohio appellate authority on conversion by denial of access, including whether demand and refusal are required when initial possession was lawful, would refine the analysis.

judge_assessments.assessment: The abstract point is correct: nominal damages become available only after conversion is established, and nominal damages cannot cure a failure of proof on liability. The brief itself expressly recognizes that sequence. But the attack then assumes away the evidence supporting wrongful dominion—continued retention, repeated denial of access, attempted retrieval, and alleged nonreturn. Source 65 supplies no relevant conversion or summary-judgment rule. Thus this does not independently support affirmance on the supplied record; it merely directs the court back to the merits of conversion.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief states that nominal damages follow only '[o]nce conversion has been established' and separately argues that repeated lockouts and retention of Alice's belongings constituted wrongful control.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The full Scales opinion and the complete Civ.R. 56 record would determine whether there was competent evidence of conversion and whether damages evidence was independently necessary.

judge_assessments.assessment: The first sentence accurately recognizes that de novo review remains confined to the Civ.R. 56 record. The rest is unsupported here. No record materials are cited to show what appellees' motion identified, whether the motion satisfied Dresher, or whether the submitted evidence affirmatively established the absence of any oral or implied rental arrangement. Sources 65 and 66 do not establish those propositions; source 66 concerns hearsay at an eviction trial, not the sufficiency of this summary-judgment record. The court cannot infer a dispositive evidentiary absence merely because the appellate brief does not discuss rent.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief correctly states the de novo standard and record limitation. It also says Alice submitted an affidavit and exhibits and that appellees could not satisfy Dresher through a conclusory assertion that she lacked evidence.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Review appellees' actual summary-judgment motion, supporting affidavit, Alice's complete affidavit and exhibits, and the trial court's stated basis for judgment.

judge_assessments.assessment: It is fair to say that the labels 'consorts' and 'house companions' do not themselves establish a statutory tenancy. But source 22 does not support the categorical assertion that Ohio law always requires rent or an express rental agreement, and the attack does not address whether an oral or implied rental agreement could exist or whether Chapter 1923 protects a broader class of occupiers. The brief's relationship facts are relevant to distinguishing sustained residence from a transient visit, even if they do not conclusively prove tenant status. The advocate risks overstating the governing law and ignoring the separate statutory theory.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief relies on Alice's prior cohabitation with Edwin, her move into Red Hill at his request, her months of residence there, and her belongings remaining there; it then characterizes her as an occupant or tenant at sufferance.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Consult the historical definitions in R.C. 5321.01 and Ohio cases involving rent-free family members, romantic partners, licensees, and implied residential rental agreements.

judge_assessments.assessment: The attack is derivative of the unsupported premise that Alice was conclusively not a tenant. Agency is not immaterial merely because the R.C. 5321.15 theory might fail: it remains relevant to attributing Cathryn's lock changes and control of Alice's belongings to Edwin, including for conversion. Moreover, the brief cites appellees' answer as admitting that Cathryn acted as Edwin's attorney in fact and Edwin's affidavit as saying he directed her to remove Alice. Source 22 does not address agency or the scope of a power of attorney. A court would not disregard this evidence as categorically irrelevant.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says the responsive pleadings admitted that Cathryn acted as Edwin's attorney in fact when changing the locks and that Edwin directed her to remove Alice.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The answer, Edwin's affidavit, and the power-of-attorney instrument would establish the precise admission, direction, and scope of authority.

judge_assessments.assessment: This could become a serious argument if the record showed that appellees identified the absence of evidence of statutory tenant status and Alice then failed to respond with qualifying evidence. The proposed attack, however, cites no record material showing what appellees actually argued or submitted. Sources 22 and 24 establish the landlord-tenant focus of R.C. 5321.15 but not that rent or a written lease was indispensable; source 65 is irrelevant. It also treats tenant status as essential to every claim, overlooking the conversion claim and the brief's separate Chapter 1923 argument. On this presentation, the court could not conclude that summary judgment was 'required.'
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief argues that appellees failed their initial Dresher burden, while Alice supplied an affidavit and exhibits showing residence, exclusion, attempted retrieval, and retention of belongings. It does not squarely establish Chapter 5321 tenant status.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The full motion, response, affidavits, complaint, and trial-court decision are necessary to determine the Dresher burden and whether tenant status was actually a pleaded and dispositive element.

judge_assessments.assessment: The brief is vulnerable because it assumes rather than demonstrates that Alice was a tenant at sufferance. But the proposed distinction of Coward is unsupported by the cited sources: neither source 2 nor source 22 supplies Coward's facts, holding, or subsequent treatment. Saying Coward involved a landlord-tenant relationship simply restates the disputed classification. Its age alone does not deprive it of force, especially where the brief cites it for a common-law proposition. The court would need the case itself before accepting this attack. If Coward is materially distinguishable or superseded, appellant's Chapter 1923 theory would be substantially weakened, but that has not been shown.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief cites Coward for the proposition that even a tenant at sufferance may be ejected only through statutory forcible-entry-and-detainer process and characterizes Alice as such a tenant.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Obtain Coward v. Fleming's full opinion, its subsequent Ohio citations, the statutory history of Chapters 1923 and 5321, and cases applying Coward to nonpaying cohabitants or licensees.

judge_assessments.assessment: The narrow observation that calling an exclusion 'wrongful' is a legal conclusion is sound, and a favorable factual inference cannot overcome a dispositive rule of law. But the proposed attack then assumes the decisive rule—that an owner may summarily exclude a residential licensee without process—which source 22 does not establish. It also assumes Alice was a mere licensee despite evidence of sustained residence at Edwin's request and appellees' later resort to an eviction notice. The court may decide status as a legal issue on undisputed facts, but it cannot reach the proposed conclusion from this authority and record alone.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief supplies underlying facts rather than relying only on the word 'wrongful': residence at Edwin's request, repeated lock changes and trespass notices, police advice to file an eviction, and a notice to quit issued after exclusion. It then argues those facts triggered Chapter 1923 and R.C. 5321.15.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Research the legal rights of a property owner against a revoked residential licensee under Ohio law and examine the full Civ.R. 56 record concerning the nature and duration of Alice's occupancy.

results.verdict: promising on the tenant-status attack, but still exposed on
results.assessment: The brief has a real strength in pressing the absence of evidence that Alice was a statutory tenant, which undercuts the R.C. 5321.15 theory. But as written it overstates that point: it treats the lack of a rental agreement or rent as decisive without showing the statutory definitions, and it does not answer the separate Chapter 1923 theory about an occupant or tenant at sufferance. Its attack on Coward is also underdeveloped because it relies on the case’s supposed facts and posture without supplying them. The brief is also vulnerable to the conversion issue, which is not solved by tenant-status arguments alone.

challenges.judge_assessment: This reaches the central weakness in the common-law theory. Source 59 reports an Eighth District rule that prior owners ordinarily lose property-related rights and obligations upon transfer, while the brief concedes that no Ohio court has adopted Restatement Section 840A. That makes reliance on nonbinding Restatement and out-of-state authorities vulnerable in this court. But the attack overstates the authority by saying Ohio affirmatively rejects all post-transfer nuisance liability. The quoted source gives only a general rule and is truncated before discussing possible exceptions; it does not address liability for a nuisance allegedly created, maintained, or concealed before transfer. The trial court also could not resolve disputed transfer facts on a pleading motion. If the court declines to extend Ohio law beyond Steele, however, appellants lose their principal common-law basis for imposing a continuing duty on Stark.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellants acknowledge that Ohio has not expressly adopted Restatement (Second) of Torts Sections 840A or 373. They are cited here for their persuasive value only, because they reflect the familiar common-law principle that one who creates or knowingly allows a nuisance to remain on land cannot automatically escape responsibility by later transferring title. The Third Party Complaint alleges that Stark knew of the lead hazard, was ordered to abate it, failed to do so, and left the premises in that condition. At the pleading stage, those allegations are enough to permit the inference that Stark's own conduct created or maintained the nuisance that later injured Ashoura Carter. Steele v. McNatt states the general rule that prior owners are divested of property-related obligations upon transfer, but it does not address and thus does not foreclose liability for a nuisance allegedly created and left unabated before transfer.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Stop saying Ohio recognizes Restatement Sections 840A and 373. Present them as persuasive authority only, and tie them to the pleaded pre-transfer creation and concealment of the nuisance, not an open-ended post-transfer duty.

challenges.judge_assessment: The attack lands substantially as to R.C. 5321.04 because that statute governs a landlord who is a party to a rental agreement, and the record alleges no rental relationship between Stark and the Carters. Source 59 also supplies adverse Eighth District authority stating the general rule that a former owner is divested of property-related obligations upon transfer. But the attack is too categorical as to the lead-control order and Cleveland ordinances. Source 59 is a secondary source whose excerpt ends before its stated qualification, and it does not establish whether an abatement order directed to Stark created an obligation or accrued tort liability that survived transfer. Nor does it establish that foreclosure retroactively extinguished a breach committed while Stark owned the property. Thus the argument is a serious challenge to the statutory-landlord theory, not a complete answer to every negligence-per-se theory asserted. If appellants cannot identify a specific provision extending the order-based duty beyond ownership, they likely lose negligence per se against Stark.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellants do not rely on R.C. 5321.04 to impose a post-transfer landlord-tenant duty on Stark. Rather, the Third Party Complaint alleges that Stark had actual notice of the lead hazard, received a specific order to abate it while it still owned the property, obtained an extension, and failed to comply before transferring the premises. Under Steele v. McNatt, prior owners are ordinarily divested of property-related obligations upon transfer absent a contrary agreement or law; but that general rule does not erase a breach already committed while Stark owned and controlled the premises. The pleaded violation of the abatement order occurred before transfer, and Stark cannot avoid liability for that completed misconduct simply by later relinquishing title.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Concede that R.C. 5321.04 does not supply a continuing landlord duty after Stark transferred title, and refocus the argument on Stark's pleaded pre-transfer breach of the City's lead-hazard order while it still owned the premises. Do not say foreclosure erased that breach; say the complaint alleges a completed violation and resulting nuisance before transfer.

challenges.opponent_argument: The complaint fails to allege facts sufficient to establish proximate cause. Under Ohio law, proximate cause requires a reasonable connection between the defendant's act and the plaintiff's injury. Source 74. The complaint alleges that Stark Group failed to abate lead hazards in 2005, but the child was poisoned years later while the Carters lived at the property under a different owner. The complaint does not allege that the lead hazard remained unabated because of Stark's failure, or that the subsequent owners did not contribute to the condition. The mere fact that Stark received an order and later the child was poisoned is too speculative to support an inference of causation. The complaint thus fails to state a claim.
challenges.why_it_matters: If the complaint does not adequately plead causation, the dismissal under Civ.R. 12(B)(6) was correct, and the appellate court should affirm.

challenges.judge_assessment: Source 74 states only the ordinary requirement of a reasonable causal connection and does not establish a heightened fact-pleading rule or support dismissal of these allegations. The attack also misreads the pleading and the brief. The complaint alleges an existing lead condition, Stark's notice and failure to correct it, continuation of that condition, and injury directly caused by the former and present owners' failure to remove or cover the lead. The brief additionally points to a later lead-control order issued to the current owner as evidence that the hazard persisted. Whether later owners contributed to the condition concerns comparative or intervening causation and does not negate pleading causation against Stark. Causation may ultimately be difficult to prove, particularly given the time and transfer, but this source and record do not justify dismissal on that ground.
challenges.suggested_response: The complaint adequately pleads proximate cause. At this stage, Appellants are not required to prove causation; they need only allege facts that, if true, permit a reasonable connection between Stark's failure to abate the lead hazard and Ashoura's injuries. The Third Party Complaint alleges that the premises contained an unsafe lead condition, that Stark had actual notice and failed to correct it after receiving an abatement order, that the dangerous condition remained on the property, and that Ashoura suffered lead poisoning as a direct and foreseeable result. The pleading further alleges that the current owner later received a similar lead-hazard order, supporting the inference that the hazardous condition persisted after Stark's failure to act. Those allegations are sufficient under Civ.R. 12(B)(6); any dispute over the relative contribution of later owners, superseding causes, or comparative fault is for later factual development, not dismissal on the pleadings.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Answer the causation challenge by leaning on the pleading standard and the complaint's own allegations: the issue is not proof at this stage, but whether the pleaded facts permit a reasonable inference that Stark's failure to abate the known hazard contributed to the injury. Keep the later-owner order only as corroboration that the hazard persisted.

judge_assessments.assessment: Burney View does not support the propositions attributed to it. Its snippet concerns summary judgment based on a legally defective eviction notice, not harmless conversion error, Civ.R. 56(F), former-owner duty, or lead-poisoning causation. On this record, the trial court expressly relied on an extra-pleading foreclosure fact while granting Civ.R. 12(B)(6) relief, and appellants had requested discovery after Stark allegedly failed to attend a deposition. An appellate court could affirm on the pleadings if every asserted legal theory fails, but it cannot simply declare summary judgment proper on an undeveloped record without addressing conversion, notice, and the pending Civ.R. 56(F) request. The harmless-error point is therefore derivative of the substantive duty arguments in a1 and a2, not an independently supported procedural attack.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief argues that Stark relied on discovery responses, that the trial court relied on a foreclosure fact contrary to the pleaded direct sale, that the motion therefore had to be confined to the pleadings or converted under Civ.R. 56, and that the court should have addressed the supported Civ.R. 56(F) request before resolving factual issues. It also argues the complaint survives even accepting the foreclosure fact.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Relevant Ohio appellate authority on harmless consideration of extra-pleading material, conversion notice, appellate affirmance on alternative grounds, and the required showing under Civ.R. 56(F) would be needed; source 80 does not address those questions.

results.assessment: As written, the brief is strongest where it treats proximate cause as a pleading question and ties the alleged lead hazard, Stark’s notice, and the later injury into a plausible chain. Its biggest weakness is the common-law nuisance theory: it leans on nonbinding Restatement and out-of-state authority even though Ohio authority cited in the challenges points the other way on post-transfer obligations, and the brief does not squarely answer that limitation. The negligence-per-se section is also vulnerable because it tries to carry post-transfer duties too far, especially beyond the landlord statute. The research leaves room on whether a pre-transfer abatement breach can survive transfer, but it does not settle that issue in Appellants’ favor.

This dismissal by the trial court is a final appealable order that affec

legal_sources.title: Ohio Eviction and Landlord-Tenant Law — 2. Final Appealable Order
legal_sources.citation: Ohio Eviction and Landlord-Tenant Law, 2022-06 (Sixth Edition), L. Jurisdictional Issues > Q. Appeal > 2. Final Appealable Order (PDF pp. 143–144)
queries: Ohio final appealable order dismissal of third-party defendant claims Civ.R. 54(B) R.C. 2505.02 no jurisdiction interlocutory order dismissal without all claims resolved

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a threshold problem the Court must examine even if appellee does not raise it. The record describes two consolidated actions, numerous counterclaims and third-party claims, and an entry dismissing only the claims between the Carters and Stark Group. Nothing supplied shows that all claims in either action were resolved or that the entry contained Civ.R. 54(B) language. The cited source supports the general proposition that judgments resolving only part of an eviction case may not be immediately appealable, but it does not establish the status of this particular docket. If unresolved claims remained and the entry lacked the required certification, the appeal must be dismissed without reaching the merits. The advocate stands to lose the present appeal, although ordinarily not the ability to appeal after a final judgment.
challenges.suggested_response: This appeal is taken from the April 19, 2010 judgment entry dismissing Appellants' claims against Stark Group in Case No. 2009 CVG 00344. Appellants submit that the entry is a final appealable order under R.C. 2505.02 and that this Court has jurisdiction to review the dismissal.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Fix the jurisdictional statement so it shows finality from the record, not just a conclusion. If the April 19, 2010 entry did not dispose of every remaining claim in the consolidated cases, the brief needs the Civ.R. 54(B) language or another final-order basis; if it cannot show that, jurisdiction is not established.

challenges.opponent_argument: Ohio law holds that prior owners are divested of all rights and obligations upon transfer of title. Steele v. McNatt, 102 Ohio App.3d 558 (8th Dist. 1995); Wiles v. Miller, 2013-Ohio-3625 (10th Dist.). Stark Group owed no duty to the Carters after the foreclosure sale, and the trial court correctly dismissed the claims.
challenges.why_it_matters: The core theory that a former owner's liability survives transfer is contrary to binding Ohio precedent, so the negligence claims fail as a matter of law.

target.excerpt: Appellants urge that this Court now recognize a property owner's liability for the harms that result from his/her failure to remediate a known lead hazard in accordance with a lawful order cannot be cut off simply because such an owner relinquishes possession of a property. Although Ohio courts have

legal_sources.title: Ohio Eviction and Landlord-Tenant Law — 6. Sale of Property, Seller’s Liability for Existing
legal_sources.citation: Ohio Eviction and Landlord-Tenant Law, 2022-06 (Sixth Edition), IX. Tenant Claims for Defective > B. R.C. 5321.04 Negligence Per Se Claim > 6. Sale of Property, Seller’s Liability for Existing (PDF pp. 478–479)

challenges.judge_assessment: Steele is Eighth District authority and creates a substantial obstacle to treating a former owner as continuing to owe ordinary landlord obligations after title transfers. The cited material, however, states the rule with an express qualification for an agreement or law establishing a contrary relationship and appears to discuss exceptions beyond the truncated excerpt. It therefore does not support the attack's categorical assertion that every possible duty and all liability necessarily ended at foreclosure. The critical question is whether Steele governs only status-based property and landlord obligations or also forecloses liability for a completed pre-transfer breach of a lead-abatement order or a continuing nuisance. The brief does not confront Steele directly. If the Court reads Steele broadly, appellants could lose their central surviving-duty theory; if it reads Steele narrowly, the lead-order and independent-tort theories remain open.
challenges.suggested_response: Stark's liability is not based on ordinary post-transfer landlord status. Appellants allege that Stark received a lawful lead-hazard control order while it still owned the property, was given time to comply, and failed to abate the hazard before relinquishing the premises. Steele recognizes the general rule only 'outside an agreement or law establishing a relationship to the contrary,' and the City of Cleveland's lead-hazard order and ordinances supplied that contrary legal duty here.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not argue that Stark stayed liable merely as a former owner after transfer. Distinguish Steele by tying liability to the pre-transfer abatement order and the City ordinance, and use Steele's own qualification that the general divestiture rule yields where a law establishes a contrary relationship.

challenges.opponent_argument: Ohio has not adopted Restatement (Second) of Torts § 840A; instead, Ohio follows the rule that a former owner's liability ceases upon transfer of title. The trial court correctly applied Ohio law, and the common law negligence claim based on the Restatement fails.
challenges.why_it_matters: The common law duty argument is unsupported by Ohio law, so the negligence claim cannot proceed.

target.excerpt: c. Appellee Stark Breached a Common Law duty to Subsequent Residents when it Relinquished Ownership of the subject premises through Foreclosure rather than Cooperating with the City in Remediating the Lead Hazards it Posed to Occupants.

legal_sources.title: Ohio Eviction and Landlord-Tenant Law — 6. Sale of Property, Seller’s Liability for Existing
legal_sources.citation: Ohio Eviction and Landlord-Tenant Law, 2022-06 (Sixth Edition), IX. Tenant Claims for Defective > B. R.C. 5321.04 Negligence Per Se Claim > 6. Sale of Property, Seller’s Liability for Existing (PDF pp. 478–479)
queries: Ohio landlord liability after sale transfer of title no duty after conveyance absent possession or control R.C. 5321.04 former landlord not liable for post-sale injuries property owner liability ends when deed delivered

challenges.judge_assessment: This attack lands substantially against the common-law portion of the brief. The brief concedes that Ohio has not adopted or interpreted Restatement Section 840A, while the cited Ohio material identifies a general rule terminating a prior owner's property-related obligations at transfer. DiCenzo's description of the Restatement as a roadmap is not adoption of Section 840A, and the numerous decisions from other jurisdictions are persuasive only. There are additional fit problems: Section 840A concerns a vendor or lessor and often focuses on a condition the transferor created or concealed, while this record describes loss through foreclosure and principally alleges failure to remediate; Section 373, as quoted by the brief, addresses risk to persons outside the land, whereas the alleged exposure occurred on the premises. Still, the cited source does not conclusively establish that Ohio rejects all continuing-nuisance liability, so affirmance is not automatic. The advocate risks losing the principal independent common-law basis for extending liability beyond transfer.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellants do not ask this Court to adopt Restatement Section 840A as a freestanding rule of Ohio law. Rather, the complaint alleges that Stark knew of the lead hazard, received a lawful abatement order, and failed to remedy the dangerous condition before transferring the property. On those allegations, Stark's own conduct created and left in place a hazardous condition whose consequences to later occupants were foreseeable.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Stop presenting Restatement § 840A as though Ohio has adopted it. Keep the common-law argument narrow: Stark allegedly knew of the hazard, was ordered to abate it, and left a dangerous condition in place before transfer, which the complaint pleads as a continuing nuisance / foreseeable-harm theory.

challenges.opponent_argument: R.C. 5321.04 imposes duties only on a 'landlord' as defined in R.C. 5321.01(B), which requires a current ownership or management role. Stark Group was not the landlord at the time of the Carters' tenancy, so no statutory duty existed and negligence per se cannot be established.
challenges.why_it_matters: The negligence per se claim collapses because the statute does not apply to former owners who are not parties to a rental agreement with the injured tenant.

target.excerpt: b. Failure to Comply with Lead Hazard Control Order Constitutes Negligence per se Under the Ohio Revised Code and/or Cleveland Codified Ordinances.

legal_sources.title: Ohio Revised Code — Ohio Rev. Code § 5321.01 — Landlord and tenant definitions.
legal_sources.citation: Ohio Rev. Code § 5321.01 (effective October 3, 2023)
queries: Ohio landlord liability after sale transfer of title no duty after conveyance absent possession or control R.C. 5321.04 former landlord not liable for post-sale injuries property owner liability ends when deed delivered

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a strong answer to the R.C. 5321.04 branch of negligence per se. R.C. 5321.01(B) defines landlord by ownership, lessor, agency, management, or rent-receiving status, and R.C. 5321.04(A), as the brief itself quotes, governs a landlord who is a party to a rental agreement. The pleaded chronology places Stark's ownership before the Carters' tenancy, with no allegation that Stark managed the premises, received their rent, or was party to their rental agreement. Shroades and Sikora establish consequences when R.C. 5321.04 applies; they do not extend the statute to a former owner outside the statutory definition. This would eliminate the R.C. 5321.04 negligence-per-se theory, but it would not by itself dispose of duties allegedly arising from a lead-control order, Cleveland ordinances, other statutes, or common law.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellants do not rely on R.C. 5321.04 to make Stark a landlord after transfer of title. The claim is that Stark had an independent statutory and ordinance-based duty to comply with the City's lead-hazard control order, and that Stark violated that duty while it still owned the premises. R.C. 5321.04 and the cases construing it confirm that Ohio imposes statutory duties on landlords; the ordinance and abatement order alleged here imposed the duty Stark is charged with breaching.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Drop the R.C. 5321.04 theory as to Stark or limit it to current landlords. Base negligence per se on the City of Cleveland lead-hazard order and ordinance language, because the statute itself does not fit a former owner who was not the Carters' landlord.

attacks_proposed.argument: The dismissal of Stark Group is not a final appealable order because the consolidated cases involve multiple parties and claims, and the trial court did not certify 'no just reason for delay' under Civ.R. 54(B). Without such certification, this Court lacks jurisdiction over the appeal.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the order is not final, the appeal must be dismissed for want of jurisdiction, ending the case.

attacks_proposed.argument: Ohio law holds that prior owners are divested of all rights and obligations upon transfer of title. Steele v. McNatt, 102 Ohio App.3d 558 (8th Dist. 1995); Wiles v. Miller, 2013-Ohio-3625 (10th Dist.). Stark Group owed no duty to the Carters after the foreclosure sale, and the trial court correctly dismissed the claims.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The core theory that a former owner's liability survives transfer is contrary to binding Ohio precedent, so the negligence claims fail as a matter of law.

attacks_proposed.argument: R.C. 5321.04 imposes duties only on a 'landlord' as defined in R.C. 5321.01(B), which requires a current ownership or management role. Stark Group was not the landlord at the time of the Carters' tenancy, so no statutory duty existed and negligence per se cannot be established.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The negligence per se claim collapses because the statute does not apply to former owners who are not parties to a rental agreement with the injured tenant.

attacks_proposed.argument: The trial court could take judicial notice of the foreclosure sale as a public record without converting the motion to one for summary judgment. Thus, the court did not err by considering that fact and ruling under Civ.R. 12(B)(6).
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The first assignment of error—that the court improperly considered matters outside the pleadings—fails, and the dismissal stands.

attacks_proposed.argument: The trial court did not abuse its discretion in failing to grant further discovery under Civ.R. 56(F) because the third-party complaint failed to state a claim as a matter of law, making any discovery futile. The request was therefore properly denied.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The procedural error claim regarding the 56(F) request fails, removing a ground for reversal.

attacks_proposed.argument: Ohio has not adopted Restatement (Second) of Torts § 840A; instead, Ohio follows the rule that a former owner's liability ceases upon transfer of title. The trial court correctly applied Ohio law, and the common law negligence claim based on the Restatement fails.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The common law duty argument is unsupported by Ohio law, so the negligence claim cannot proceed.

attacks_proposed.argument: Even if a duty could be found, the complaint fails to allege facts showing that Stark Group's failure to abate was the proximate cause of the injuries, given the intervening ownership and the current landlord's independent duty to maintain the premises. The chain of causation is too attenuated as a matter of law.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The causation element of negligence is not satisfied, providing an independent ground to affirm the dismissal.

attacks_proposed.argument: The issue is not one of first impression; Ohio courts have already held that prior owners are not liable after transfer. The trial court's decision is consistent with existing law, and no new rule is needed.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The appeal's premise that the Court should recognize a new duty is unfounded, and the existing precedent supports affirmance.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is a threshold problem the Court must examine even if appellee does not raise it. The record describes two consolidated actions, numerous counterclaims and third-party claims, and an entry dismissing only the claims between the Carters and Stark Group. Nothing supplied shows that all claims in either action were resolved or that the entry contained Civ.R. 54(B) language. The cited source supports the general proposition that judgments resolving only part of an eviction case may not be immediately appealable, but it does not establish the status of this particular docket. If unresolved claims remained and the entry lacked the required certification, the appeal must be dismissed without reaching the merits. The advocate stands to lose the present appeal, although ordinarily not the ability to appeal after a final judgment.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The jurisdictional statement asserts that the dismissal is a final appealable order under Article IV, Section 3 and R.C. 2505.03, but it does not address the remaining claims, the effect of consolidation, R.C. 2505.02, or Civ.R. 54(B).
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The complete April 19, 2010 judgment entry and docket are necessary to determine whether all claims and parties were resolved or whether the entry included an express finding of no just reason for delay.

judge_assessments.assessment: Steele is Eighth District authority and creates a substantial obstacle to treating a former owner as continuing to owe ordinary landlord obligations after title transfers. The cited material, however, states the rule with an express qualification for an agreement or law establishing a contrary relationship and appears to discuss exceptions beyond the truncated excerpt. It therefore does not support the attack's categorical assertion that every possible duty and all liability necessarily ended at foreclosure. The critical question is whether Steele governs only status-based property and landlord obligations or also forecloses liability for a completed pre-transfer breach of a lead-abatement order or a continuing nuisance. The brief does not confront Steele directly. If the Court reads Steele broadly, appellants could lose their central surviving-duty theory; if it reads Steele narrowly, the lead-order and independent-tort theories remain open.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief argues that the lead-control order, Cleveland ordinances, negligence principles, and Restatement nuisance rules imposed a duty that could not be terminated by relinquishing title. It cites out-of-state cases and admits that no Ohio case expressly recognizes the proposed former-owner liability, but it does not discuss Steele or Wiles.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The full opinions in Steele v. McNatt and Wiles v. Miller, including the nature and timing of the alleged breaches, are needed to determine whether their transfer rule reaches accrued tort liability and continuing-nuisance claims.

judge_assessments.assessment: This attack lands substantially against the common-law portion of the brief. The brief concedes that Ohio has not adopted or interpreted Restatement Section 840A, while the cited Ohio material identifies a general rule terminating a prior owner's property-related obligations at transfer. DiCenzo's description of the Restatement as a roadmap is not adoption of Section 840A, and the numerous decisions from other jurisdictions are persuasive only. There are additional fit problems: Section 840A concerns a vendor or lessor and often focuses on a condition the transferor created or concealed, while this record describes loss through foreclosure and principally alleges failure to remediate; Section 373, as quoted by the brief, addresses risk to persons outside the land, whereas the alleged exposure occurred on the premises. Still, the cited source does not conclusively establish that Ohio rejects all continuing-nuisance liability, so affirmance is not automatic. The advocate risks losing the principal independent common-law basis for extending liability beyond transfer.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief expressly acknowledges that no Ohio case has adopted Section 840A, relies on DiCenzo for Ohio courts' general use of the Restatement, invokes Sections 840A and 373, and cites Massachusetts and other out-of-state nuisance decisions.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Research should address whether any Ohio appellate decision has adopted Sections 840A or 373, recognized post-transfer liability for a nuisance created or maintained by a former owner, or applied those principles following an involuntary foreclosure.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is a strong answer to the R.C. 5321.04 branch of negligence per se. R.C. 5321.01(B) defines landlord by ownership, lessor, agency, management, or rent-receiving status, and R.C. 5321.04(A), as the brief itself quotes, governs a landlord who is a party to a rental agreement. The pleaded chronology places Stark's ownership before the Carters' tenancy, with no allegation that Stark managed the premises, received their rent, or was party to their rental agreement. Shroades and Sikora establish consequences when R.C. 5321.04 applies; they do not extend the statute to a former owner outside the statutory definition. This would eliminate the R.C. 5321.04 negligence-per-se theory, but it would not by itself dispose of duties allegedly arising from a lead-control order, Cleveland ordinances, other statutes, or common law.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief quotes the statutory limitation to a landlord who is a party to a rental agreement, then relies on Shroades and Sikora to characterize violations as negligence per se. It does not explain how Stark qualified as the Carters' landlord after transferring the property.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The version of R.C. 5321.01 and R.C. 5321.04 effective during the alleged events should be checked, along with any Ohio authority applying those provisions to a former landlord's pre-transfer breach.

judge_assessments.assessment: The cited source does not support the proposition that an Ohio court may take judicial notice of a foreclosure sale and use it to resolve a Civ.R. 12(B)(6) motion without conversion. On this record, the complaint alleged a direct sale, while the trial court found a sheriff's sale and used that different fact to invoke the foreclosure exception. The brief squarely argues that this fact came from outside the pleadings and cites authority limiting a pleadings motion to the pleadings. Whether a foreclosure docket falls within a recognized judicial-notice exception requires authority not supplied here. As presented, the attack would not defeat the first assignment of error.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief cites Flanagan, Nelson, Barilatz, and Peterson for the rule that a pleadings motion is restricted to the pleadings, identifies the foreclosure finding as contrary to the pleaded transfer, and argues that reliance on it required summary-judgment treatment.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Ohio appellate authority specifically addressing judicial notice of court dockets, deeds, and foreclosure records on Civ.R. 12(B)(6) or 12(C) review would be required.

judge_assessments.assessment: The cited source is a local-rule excerpt unrelated to Civ.R. 56(F), discovery continuances, or futility, so it does not support the proposed attack. The record also says appellants submitted counsel's affidavit identifying a noticed deposition that Stark failed to attend and the facts they expected to develop. Moreover, if the trial court truly decided only a Civ.R. 12(B)(6) motion, Civ.R. 56(F) was not the governing mechanism; if it relied on outside evidence and effectively converted the motion, the failure to address a supported discovery request becomes more significant. Futility depends on first establishing that every pleaded legal theory fails, which this attack merely assumes.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief states that counsel submitted an affidavit, that Stark failed to attend a noticed organizational deposition, and that the requested discovery concerned duty, breach, causation, Stark's relationship to the foreclosing party, and whether foreclosure was deliberately allowed.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Relevant authority would need to address Ohio Civ.R. 56(F)'s affidavit requirements, implicit denial of a continuance, and whether discovery may be denied as futile after conversion from Civ.R. 12 to Civ.R. 56.

judge_assessments.assessment: The cited source addresses former-owner obligations, not proximate cause or superseding causation. The complaint expressly alleges that Stark's failure to disclose or remediate caused the child's poisoning and that present and former owners acted as joint tortfeasors. At the pleading stage those allegations and reasonable inferences are accepted as true. Intervening ownership and a later landlord's maintenance duty may become substantial comparative-fault or superseding-cause issues, but the supplied authority does not establish that they break causation as a matter of law. The brief's causal allegations are sparse and may face proof problems later, but this attack does not furnish an independent pleading-stage ground for affirmance.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief quotes allegations that the third-party defendants' failure to disclose, remove, or cover the lead hazards caused the injuries; alleges Stark knew of and failed to obey the order; and argues that causation is ordinarily for the factfinder.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Authority on Ohio superseding cause, subsequent owners' negligence, and pleading causation in lead-exposure cases would be necessary to strengthen this argument.

judge_assessments.assessment: The cited material establishes only a general rule concerning prior owners' rights and obligations after transfer. It does not show that an Ohio court has decided the narrower question identified by the brief: whether a known, unremediated lead hazard subject to a governmental control order can support liability to later occupants after foreclosure. The brief expressly distinguishes that question and acknowledges the absence of Ohio authority. Whether the matter is formally one of first impression has little independent effect on the outcome; the Court must still determine the scope of Steele and any order-based or nuisance duty. This attack overstates the source and would add little beyond attacks a2 and a6.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief characterizes the precise lead-order and subsequent-occupant issue as one of first impression, while acknowledging existing Ohio landlord-liability law and the lack of an Ohio decision adopting its proposed former-owner rule.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: A directly analogous Ohio decision involving a former owner, a pre-transfer lead-abatement order, and injury to later tenants would be needed to disprove the first-impression characterization.

results.assessment: The brief has a workable core, especially on the R.C. 5321.04 point, where the research supports that Stark was not a landlord at the relevant time. But it is still vulnerable in two major places: first, the jurisdictional statement may be wrong if unresolved claims remained and Civ.R. 54(B) language was absent; second, the brief does not squarely answer Steele’s rule that a former owner’s obligations generally end at transfer of title. The common-law/Restatement theory is also shaky because Ohio has not adopted Section 840A. The research leaves open whether any continuing-duty or nuisance theory survives those limits.

challenges.opponent_argument: The brief's claim that a repair-based defense is unavailable without prior rent escrow under R.C. 5321.07 overlooks the defense provided by R.C. 1923.061(B). Under that statute, a tenant may raise the landlord's violations of the rental agreement or R.C. Chapter 5321 as a defense to eviction for nonpayment, and the court has discretion to order rent deposit. The tenant is not required to have previously deposited rent. Thus, the trial court could have considered Ealy's repair evidence even absent escrow, and the brief's contrary assertion misstates the law.
challenges.why_it_matters: If the repair defense was available under R.C. 1923.061(B), the trial court's exclusion of that evidence or failure to consider it could constitute reversible error, undermining the appellee's argument that no valid defense existed.

challenges.judge_assessment: The attack identifies a real overstatement in u40. The retrieved authorities indicate that R.C. 1923.061(B) permits a tenant defending a nonpayment eviction to rely on a landlord's violation of the rental agreement or R.C. Chapter 5321, and that any deposit ordered under that provision is discretionary. That materially undercuts the brief's categorical assertion that premises-condition evidence is unavailable unless the tenant previously used the R.C. 5321.07 escrow procedure. The brief does, however, say that Ealy was allowed to present repair evidence and that the trial court considered it but found no meritorious defense. With no transcript, the appellate court cannot determine whether evidence was actually excluded, what violations were proved, whether the statutory defense was properly pleaded, or whether any setoff could eliminate the rent default. The appellee therefore stands to lose its categorical legal rationale, but not necessarily the affirmance; the incomplete record and absence of demonstrated prejudice remain substantial answers.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellant’s repair argument does not undo the judgment. Ohio law recognizes that, in an eviction action for nonpayment of rent, a landlord’s violation of the rental agreement or R.C. Chapter 5321 may be raised under R.C. 1923.061(B), and the court may order a rent deposit in its discretion. But that does not help Appellant here: the record shows that he admitted the rent was unpaid, did not deposit rent with the court, and the trial court permitted him to present evidence before finding that he had failed to establish a valid defense. Without a transcript, Appellant cannot show that the court excluded admissible evidence, misapplied R.C. 1923.061(B), or that any alleged repair issue would have defeated STJ’s right to possession.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Revise the repair-defense discussion to stop saying that rent escrow under R.C. 5321.07 is an absolute prerequisite in every case. A tenant may assert a landlord-violation defense under R.C. 1923.061(B), but the record here still does not show that Appellant established such a defense or any prejudice from the trial court’s ruling.

challenges.opponent_argument: The brief assumes that STJ's three-day notice was valid and properly served, but a valid notice under R.C. 1923.04 is a jurisdictional prerequisite for a forcible entry and detainer action. The brief provides no details about the content or method of service, and without a transcript, the appellate court cannot verify that the notice complied with the statutory requirements. The appellee bears the burden to establish jurisdiction, and the conclusory assertion in the brief is insufficient to support the trial court's judgment.
challenges.why_it_matters: If the notice was defective, the trial court lacked subject matter jurisdiction, rendering the writ of restitution void. This directly attacks the foundation of the appellee's merits argument.

The brief does not omit the method of service: it states that the June 14 notice was left at the premises, a method expressly permitted by R.C. 1923.04, and it identifies the notice as Exhibit A to the complaint. results.verdict: Mostly persuasive, but vulnerable on the repair-defense law
results.assessment: The brief largely holds up on the notice issues: it identifies the statutory notice, states service was made by leaving it at the premises, and the attacks do not point to any concrete defect in timing, language, or service. The main weakness is the categorical statement that repair-based defenses are unavailable absent prior rent escrow; that overstates the law and should be narrowed because R.C. 1923.061(B) allows a tenant to raise landlord violations as a defense. Even so, the incomplete record and lack of a transcript still blunt the challenge, so the judgment is not clearly undone. The missing-language attack is especially weak because it never identifies an omitted statutory phrase.
